chapter_theme: Fear of evil deeds is presented as a mark of excellence and as enlightened self-interest. Harm done to others does not stay with them: it pursues the doer as surely as a shadow, so whoever loves himself will refrain.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: why evil deeds should be feared (201-203), how those who harm others are themselves ruined (204-209), and the safety of the one who doesn't (210).

201.reading: Those given to evil deeds don't fear the intoxication called evil deed; the excellent do.
201.nuance: Fear is the sign of moral standing here, not a weakness. Parimelazhagar adds an insight about habit: long practice has removed the fear in one group, and never having done such things keeps it alive in the other.

positions.position: செருக்கு is delusion: the evil deed is called by the name of the confusion it brings on.
செருக்கு is the elation of wrongdoing.
செருக்கு is a pleasure the deed may yield, and the wise fear the deed even so.

202.reading: Since evil deeds yield evil, they are to be feared more than fire.
202.nuance: The verse's reason is only that evil begets evil, sounded in the play of தீயவை on தீ. Parimelazhagar supplies a further reason, that fire does not burn across time, place and bodies, which brings in rebirth that the verse doesn't state.

positions.position: Fire can't burn in another time, another place or another body, and an evil deed can.
positions.quote: பிறிதொரு காலத்தும், பிறிதொரு தேயத்தும், பிறிதோர் உடம்பினும் சென்று சுடுதல் தீக்கு இன்மையின்

203.reading: They say the chief of all understanding is to leave off doing harm even to those who hate you.
203.nuance: The word is அறிவு, not virtue as Pope's gloss has it. Forbearance appears here as the height of intelligence, and Parimelazhagar makes the logic prudential: refraining keeps suffering from coming back to oneself.

positions.position: It is the chief understanding because one infers that refraining, even when able to strike, keeps suffering away.
positions.quote: செய்யத் தக்குழியுஞ் செய்யாது ஒழியவே தமக்குத் துன்பம் வாராது என உய்த்துணர்தலின்

204.reading: Don't plot another's ruin even by a lapse; if you do, அறம் plots the ruin of the plotter.
204.nuance: The same verb, சூழ், serves both parties, so the plotting already sets the reply in motion and harm need never be carried out. Parimelazhagar draws the point: even thinking of it is forbidden.

positions.position: அறம் is a deity of virtue, and its 'plotting' is resolving to leave the man to his ruin.
positions.quote: அறக்கடவுள் எண்ணுதலாவது, அவன் கெடத் தான் நீங்க நினைத்தல்.

positions.position: அறம் actively returns harm for harm, and gets in before the intended victim can respond.
positions.quote: தீமை செய்தார்க்குத் தீமை பயக்கும் அறந்தானே சூழும்

positions.position: சூழும் means surrounds: moral order closes in on him like a siege.

205.reading: Don't do evil saying 'I have nothing'; if you do, you'll have nothing all over again.
205.nuance: The verse answers the strongest excuse for wrongdoing on its own terms: it doesn't defend the poor man's honour but says the plan won't work. Parimelazhagar also reports other glossators who take the second poverty as poverty of good qualities.

positions.position: The poverty returns across lives, birth after birth.
positions.quote: அத் தீவினையால் பிறவிதோறும் இலன் ஆம் என்பதாம்.

positions.position: The deed simply fails to produce wealth, with no appeal to rebirth.
positions.quote: பின்பும் நல்குரவினனாவன்; அது செல் வம் பயவாது

206.reading: One who doesn't want afflicting things to overpower him should not do evil things to others.
206.nuance: The balance of தீப்பால and நோய்ப்பால gives the rule its shape: what one portions out as evil returns as a portion of pain.

207.reading: However great the enmity they've incurred, people survive it; the enmity of deeds doesn't die and follows them to kill.
207.nuance: The deed is made an enemy of a special kind, one that can't be outrun because it travels with the doer. Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss it as entering wherever one enters.

208.reading: The ruin of those who do evil is like a person's shadow, which never perishes and stays at the foot.
208.nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a shadow that stretches far but comes back to rest at the foot, so a consequence can seem distant and still be right there. He expressly rejects another reading, in which the shadow stands for a deed latent until its time.

positions.position: The image is the shadow's return to the foot, not a deed lying hidden until its season.
positions.quote: ஒருவன் நிழல் நொடிதாகப் போயும், அவன்றன்னை விடாது வந்து அடியின்கண் தங்கி தன்மைத்து.

209.reading: If a person loves himself, let him not go near the portion of evil deeds, however small.
209.nuance: The appeal rests on self-love, using காதலன், a word of real attachment. The verse doesn't ask a person to overcome self-regard: it asks him to think it through, and on Parimelazhagar's reading harm to others is harm to oneself.

210.reading: Know that one who doesn't stray aside and do evil is a person for whom ruin is rare.
210.nuance: அருங்கேடன் on its face says ruin is 'rare' or 'hard'. Parimelazhagar argues that அருமை here means absence, which turns a strong probability into a guarantee. Kalaignar also says no ruin at all.

positions.position: அருமை means absence, so the man has no ruin at all.

links.note: 201 makes fear the mark of the excellent; 1075 makes fear the conduct of the base. They can be reconciled only by asking what is feared, which suggests that fear of the deed and fear of the penalty are morally different things.
203 only asks one to refrain from harming an enemy. 314 goes further and makes kindness to the wrongdoer the punishment itself. Prudent restraint becomes active shaming.

205 argues that wrongdoing won't cure poverty. 657 removes that premise: even when wealth does come through blame, the poverty of the worthy is better. Moral refusal doesn't depend on the prediction in 205.
They give the same rule different grounds. 206 rests on what will come back to you, 316 on knowing from your own experience what hurts. One argues from consequence and the other from fellow-feeling.
Two pursuers that can't be evaded: the deed follows from behind (பின் சென்று) and fate arrives first (முந்துறும்). Together they close off escape in both directions.
Both turn on தன்னைத்தான், making care for the self the argument for restraint: from evil deeds here, from anger in 305.
210 says the upright man's ruin is absent or rare. 169 admits that this ruin does occur and is something to ponder. The Kural keeps the moral promise and the troubling fact side by side.

source_issues: 208: the verse text reads அஇஉறைந் தற்று, an evident corruption. Parimelazhagar's அடி உறைந்தற்று and Pope's 'heels' show that the word should be அடியுறைந் தற்று.
202, 209, 210: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
